Goings-on means activities, events, or things that are happening — especially ones that seem strange, suspicious, morally questionable, or at least worth talking about.

Think of it as someone watching a situation and noting down everything that's taking place — usually with a sense of curiosity, amusement, or mild disapproval.

This is the most important thing to understand: goings-on is rarely neutral. It almost always carries one of these flavours:

  • Suspicion — something seems off here
  • Disapproval — this behaviour is not quite right
  • Amusement or gossip — look at all this drama
  • Mild scandal — people are doing things they probably shouldn't

When someone uses "goings-on," they are often hinting that the activities in question are a little shady, odd, or improper — even if they don't say so directly.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "There are some strange events happening at that office." — neutral, factual
  • "There are some strange goings-on at that office." — the same information, but now it sounds like you are half-suspicious, half-gossiping. There's a wink in the word.
It is always plural — without exception

You will never say "a going-on." The word simply does not exist in singular form. It is always goings-on, and it always takes a plural verb.

✅ These goings-on are very suspicious.
✅ The goings-on in that building worry me.
❌ This going-on is strange.
❌ A going-on occurred.
Register: who uses it, and when

Goings-on is informal and colloquial. It belongs to everyday speech and casual writing — not to formal reports, academic writing, or official documents.

It also has a slightly old-fashioned or traditional flavour. It's the kind of word a nosy neighbour, a gossipy aunt, or a disapproving elder might use. That said, it is still fully current and understood by all English speakers today. It's especially common in British English, though Americans use it too.

Goings-on is very frequently paired with adjectives that signal strangeness or suspicion:

  • strange goings-on
  • odd goings-on
  • mysterious goings-on
  • funny goings-on (funny here means suspicious, not humorous)
  • unsavoury goings-on
  • political goings-on
  • sexual goings-on

It is also common to say:

  • "I don't like these goings-on." (disapproval)
  • "She kept track of all the goings-on in the village." (gossiping/reporting)
  • "There were some interesting goings-on last night." (hinting at drama)

1. The neighbours noticed some suspicious goings-on at the old warehouse — men arriving late at night, lights flickering, boxes being unloaded.
→ Here it signals something shady and secretive.

2. She disapproved of the goings-on at her son's college parties.
→ Disapproval of behaviour she considers inappropriate.

3. The documentary gave viewers a fascinating look at the backstage goings-on of a royal palace.
→ More neutral here — just the behind-the-scenes activities — but still implies that these are things not usually seen or talked about.

4. "I don't know what goings-on you've been up to while I was away, but this house is a mess!"
→ Mild accusation, slightly humorous tone.

5. The journalist spent a year investigating the financial goings-on inside the corporation.
→ Implies irregular or questionable financial activities.

6. She sat by the window all day, watching the goings-on in the street below.
→ Just observing the activity and events of daily life — fairly neutral, more like people-watching.

• It does not mean the act of leaving or departing (even though "going" can mean that in other contexts). Here, it is completely unrelated to movement or travel.
  • It does not always mean something criminal — just something worth noting, and often something slightly irregular or unusual.

Imagine a gossipy person peering through their curtains, watching the neighbourhood, and later telling a friend: "Oh, you should have seen the goings-on next door last night!"

That image — of watchful curiosity, mild scandal, and the sense that something is happening that perhaps shouldn't be — is the heart of the word.

In one sentence: Goings-on means the (usually odd, suspicious, or noteworthy) events and activities happening in a place or situation — always used in the plural, always in an informal register, and almost always with a hint of curiosity or disapproval baked in.
